summary: This standards-track memo describes using the Cryptographic Message Syntax to protect firmware packages, which contain code for hardware modules. A digital signature protects against undetected modification, and encryption can be used for confidentiality.

plainLanguage.summary: Updates for a device should come with a seal that shows nobody tampered with them. This document explains how to put that seal on firmware.

subtitle: How to wrap a firmware update in signed, optionally encrypted CMS so a device only runs code from sources it trusts.

tldr.problem: A hardware module, especially a cryptographic one, must not run firmware that was tampered with or that comes from an unknown source. Some firmware must also stay secret in transit.
tldr.mechanism: The firmware package is treated as an opaque binary and wrapped in Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS). It is optionally compressed and encrypted, then always digitally signed with a required set of signed attributes. The module can also return a signed or unsigned load receipt or error report.
tldr.outcome: A bootstrap loader in the module accepts only packages whose signature chains to an installed trust anchor and which match its hardware type, community and version rules. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has no obsoleting or updating RFC listed.

today: RFC 4108 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2005, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Protecting Firmware with CMS
sections.content:
RFC 4108 describes how to use the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) to protect firmware packages, which hold object code for one or more programmable components of a hardware module. It was written with cryptographic hardware modules in mind, because they have strong security requirements, but the package can be associated with any hardware module.

The firmware package itself is an opaque binary object. A digital signature protects it from undetected modification and provides data origin authentication. Encryption is optional and protects it from disclosure; compression is optional and shrinks it. When all three are used, the package is compressed, then encrypted, then signed.

The RFC does not define a physical interface or a loading protocol. It names portable memory devices, file transfer and web pages as possible delivery mechanisms, and only fixes the format that must be presented to the module.
sections.plainLanguage: A device update is like a parcel. This document says how to seal the parcel so the device can check who sent it and that nobody opened it on the way.

sections.title: Hardware Module, Loader and Trust Anchors
sections.content:
The architecture has three parts: the hardware module, the firmware package and a bootstrap loader. The loader must have access to one or more trust anchors, which are trusted public keys used to check the package signature. One or more trust anchors MUST be installed in non-volatile memory before deployment, so the trust anchors define who can create firmware for the module.

A trust anchor consists of a public key signature algorithm and key, plus a public key identifier. It can verify the package signature directly, or it can validate an X.509 certification path whose final certificate holds the signing key. Using a path requires an X.500 distinguished name for the trust anchor.

Each hardware module type and revision MUST be named by a unique object identifier. Modules SHOULD have a unique permanent serial number, and MUST have one if they generate receipts or error reports. The loader MUST reject a package if it cannot validate the signature, if the module type is not in the package's target list, if the module is not in a listed community, or if it cannot decrypt the package.

Modules may be unable to fetch certificates or revocation data. So the signer SHOULD include the certificates needed to build a path, and any extra revocation checking is left to the party loading the package.
sections.plainLanguage: The toy has a tiny guard at the door who keeps a list of trusted seals. The guard turns away any box with a wrong seal, a wrong toy name or a lock the toy has no key for.

sections.title: The Layered Package Format
sections.content:
The outermost CMS ContentInfo MUST always be present and MUST encapsulate SignedData. If the package is encrypted, the SignedData MUST encapsulate EncryptedData. If it is compressed, the layer just inside the signature or the encryption MUST be CompressedData. At the centre is the new FirmwarePkgData content type, which is a plain octet string identified by id-ct-firmwarePackage (1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1.16).

The signature layer has strict rules. SignedData and SignerInfo versions MUST be 3, there MUST be a single digest algorithm and exactly one SignerInfo, and the signer identifier alternative subjectKeyIdentifier MUST be supported by the loader. Signed attributes are required, and the set MUST be DER encoded. Extended certificates and attribute certificates MUST NOT be included, and CRLs SHOULD NOT be included.

The EncryptedData version MUST be 0 and its unprotectedAttrs MUST NOT be present. The CompressedData version MUST also be 0. Digitally signed structures MUST be DER encoded; other structures do not need DER, although definite length encoding is strongly RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like nesting boxes. The outer box carries the seal, the next box is locked, the next is squashed small, and the update is in the middle. You can skip the locked or squashed boxes, but never the seal.

sections.title: Signed Attributes
sections.content:
The signer MUST sign a collection of attributes along with the package. Four are mandatory: content-type, message-digest, firmware-package-identifier and target-hardware-module-identifiers. If the package is encrypted, decrypt-key-identifier MUST also be included, naming the symmetric key needed. If the package is for specific communities, community-identifiers MUST be included.

Several others are SHOULD: firmware-package-message-digest (computed before any compression, encryption or signing), signing-time, content-hints and signing-certificate. Packages that depend on other packages SHOULD carry firmware-package-info with a dependencies field. implemented-crypto-algorithms and implemented-compress-algorithms MAY list algorithms the package exposes to applications.

A package is named in one of two ways. A legacy name is an unstructured octet string. A preferred name is an object identifier plus a version number, which MUST be a monotonically increasing non-negative integer. Implementations MUST ignore signed attributes they do not recognize.
sections.plainLanguage: The signed label on the box says what it is, which toy it fits, and which version it is. The seal covers the label too, so nobody can change it without breaking the seal.

sections.title: Decryption Keys and Unsigned Attributes
sections.content:
If the package is encrypted, the firmware-decryption key must reach the module over a secure path. The RFC leaves this open, saying the key might arrive via physical media or an independent electronic path. It also defines one optional mechanism.

The only unsigned attribute allowed is wrapped-firmware-decryption-key, and at most one instance. Because the signature does not cover it, any party in the distribution chain can replace it, which lets the key be wrapped with a different key-encryption key for each link. Its value is a CMS EnvelopedData with no encrypted content of its own; the key sits in recipientInfos, and the encrypted content is the one in the EncryptedData structure. Key transport, key agreement, symmetric key-encryption keys and passwords are supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The key to open the locked box can travel separately, or be tucked into a pocket on the outside that anyone along the way can swap for a pocket made just for the next person.

sections.title: Stale Versions and Dependencies
sections.content:
If a package with a disastrous flaw is released, a later package MAY designate a stale version, and the loader SHOULD then refuse that version and anything earlier. The module keeps a list of stale versions in non-volatile storage. With preferred names, a new package is rejected when its object identifier matches and its version is less than or equal to a stale version number. Loading an earlier version over a later one SHOULD generate a warning.

The RFC admits this cannot be complete protection: storage is limited, so a user can load other package types with their own stale versions until the stored entries are pushed out, then load the flawed one. It keeps the feature because many modules have very few packages written for them.

Packages normally SHOULD be complete firmware loads. If a package depends on others, it MUST identify them, and the loader MUST reject a load if a dependency is unavailable or if loading it would leave an already loaded package's dependencies unsatisfied.
sections.plainLanguage: If one version of the instructions was bad, the maker can say never go back to it. The toy has only a small notebook for such notes, though, so a clever person might fill the notebook up and sneak the bad version in.

sections.title: Load Receipts and Error Reports
sections.content:
Modules MAY report back. A firmware package load receipt says a package loaded successfully; a firmware package load error says it did not. Support for both is OPTIONAL, and each can be signed (RECOMMENDED) or unsigned. A module that generates either MUST have a unique serial number, and one that signs them MUST have a private signature key and a certificate or its designator.

The receipt carries the hardware type, serial number and package name, plus optionally the trust anchor key identifier and the decrypt key identifier. The decrypt key identifier MUST NOT be included unless the package was encrypted and successfully decrypted. Receipts let an operator find which modules need an updated package when a flaw is found.

The error report adds an errorCode, an optional vendorErrorCode (which MUST be present when the code is otherError), an optional package name and an optional list describing the current firmware configuration. Signed reports and receipts must include the content-type and message-digest attributes, and the signing-time attribute SHOULD be included if the module has a real-time clock.

A signing certificate for a module identifies it through a critical subject alternative name of type otherName, using a hardware module name made of the hardware type and serial number. The subject distinguished name is empty.
sections.plainLanguage: After the toy tries the update it can send a note back saying it worked, or saying exactly what went wrong, and it can sign the note so you know it is really from that toy.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The CMS security considerations apply here too. This document adds a few of its own. Private signature keys must be protected: if the firmware-signing key is compromised, outsiders can create packages that modules accept, and if a module's key is compromised, outsiders can forge receipts and error reports. A leaked firmware-decryption key can disclose the package.

Algorithms weaken over time, and replacing them through a firmware update can cause interoperability failures, so old and new algorithms generally need to be supported together during a transition. Encrypted packages need keys from a good random source, and the RFC points to RFC 4086 for guidance.

The stale-version feature has limits (see the stale versions section), and community identifiers are only as trustworthy as the mechanism that assigns community membership, which the RFC does not specify.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole system is only as safe as the secret stamps and keys. If a thief steals the maker's stamp, the toy cannot tell real updates from fake ones.

viz.caption: SOME LOAD ERROR CODES (SELECTED FROM THE RFC)

items.label: decodeFailure
items.desc: The ASN.1 decode of the package failed.

items.label: notAuthorized
items.desc: The signer leads to a trust anchor that is not an authorized signer.

items.label: signatureFailure
items.desc: The signature could not be validated.

items.label: noDecryptKey
items.desc: The module lacks the named decryption key.

items.label: wrongHardware
items.desc: The module is not in the target hardware list.

items.label: stalePackage
items.desc: The package is rejected because it is stale.

items.label: notInCommunity
items.desc: The module is not in the listed community.

items.label: insufficientMemory
items.desc: The module did not have enough memory.

items.label: breaksDependency
items.desc: Loading would break another package's dependency.

items.label: otherError
items.desc: Anything else; a vendor error code MUST then be present.
